analysis.one_liner: Blocked federal agencies from enforcing new coal-mining permit review policies until they went through formal rulemaking.
analysis.headline: The bill, which drew 17 cosponsors including 5 Democrats, never received a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2009 and 2010, the EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers began coordinating more closely on permits for Appalachian surface coal mining, and EPA issued guidance tightening its review of those mines under the Clean Water Act. This bill would have cut off federal funding for carrying out those two documents, effectively suspending them, unless each agency first wrote formal regulations through the full public rulemaking process. It was introduced by Rep. Hal Rogers of Kentucky with 17 cosponsors from both parties, referred to three House committees, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Appalachian surface coal mining companies were the direct beneficiaries: the bill would have neutralized the 2009 memorandum and 2010 guidance that the EPA was using to review, delay, and sometimes block their Clean Water Act permits [S2][S3]. Coal mining towns whose jobs depend on those operations would have gained if, as the bill's findings claimed, about 17,806 jobs and 81 small businesses were at risk from the delayed permits [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It barred the EPA, the Army Corps of Engineers, and the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement from spending any money to implement or enforce the June 2009 permit-coordination memorandum or the April 2010 Appalachian mining review guidance until each agency issued a formal regulation through public notice-and-comment rulemaking [S2][S3].

The bill's stated purpose was to restore federal permitting of Appalachian surface coal mines to the way it worked before the new procedures, which its findings said had delayed Clean Water Act permits for 190 mining operations expected to produce over 2 billion tons of coal and support roughly 17,806 mining jobs and 81 small businesses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill had passed, communities downstream of Appalachian surface mines would have borne the cost: the EPA and the Corps would have had to stand down from the coordinated Clean Water Act review of mountaintop-removal and valley-fill permits, allowing mining projects affecting streams and water quality to proceed with less federal scrutiny [S2]. Because the agencies were not required to ever write the formal rules, the suspension could have lasted indefinitely [S3].

drawbacks.text: Passing the bill would have ended the EPA-Corps coordination procedures and the April 2010 review guidance, the federal tools that had been reviewing and, in some cases, blocking or delaying Appalachian surface-mining permits, including the 190 permits the bill itself cites [S2][S3].

Coal communities and environmental groups viewed the June 2009 memorandum and April 2010 guidance as overdue enforcement of the Clean Water Act against mountaintop-removal mining, which buries streams and degrades water quality in downstream communities; cutting off funding for that review would have removed that protection without any replacement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's procedural argument had real force: both documents were written as memoranda or guidance rather than rules, and the Administrative Procedure Act generally requires public notice and comment before agencies set binding policy, so asking for rulemaking is not a frivolous demand [S2][S3]. But the practical effect of the bill was to switch off a coordinated federal review of Appalachian surface-mining permits indefinitely, since agencies could simply decline to write the rules, leaving permits that affect streams and valley fills to move with less federal scrutiny [S2]. The bill's own economic claims rested on agency figures about delayed permits, not independent analysis, and it offered no substitute for the water-quality review it would have defunded [S3]. On balance, the costs to communities near the mines outweighed the procedural gain, and the electricity-reliability framing was a stretch for a bill about one agency's permitting guidance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees, sent to a subcommittee, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 14, 2010 and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources Committees the same day [S5].
The only follow-up action was a referral to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee on September 15, 2010; no markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and all House bills not passed die automatically at that point [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's enhanced review of Appalachian surface-mining permits stayed in place, and communities near the mines kept the federal water-quality scrutiny the bill would have cut off; coal operators did not get the relief the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: EPA's permit review, and communities near the mines

for.role: U.S. Representatives from West Virginia and Virginia; original cosponsors from coal districts
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from Appalachian coal-state Democrats [S3].

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but heavily Republican: 12 of 178 House Republicans cosponsored versus 5 of 253 House Democrats, and no vote was ever taken [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have cut off funding for the EPA-Corps coordination procedures and the EPA review guidance that were delaying or blocking the companies' Clean Water Act mining permits, letting permits proceed with less federal scrutiny [S2][S3]. Coal operators were the bill's intended beneficiary and the source of its jobs figures [S3].

The bill was framed as protecting electricity reliability by keeping roughly a two-year supply of Appalachian coal from being held up by permitting delays [S3]. Utilities burning that coal would benefit from steadier, cheaper fuel supply.
